name: Chapter 8: Mechanical Properties of Solids
description: Elasticity, stress and strain, Hooke’s law, stress-strain curve, Young’s, shear and bulk moduli, Poisson’s ratio, elastic energy, applications

cards.term: Are real solids perfectly rigid?
cards.definition: No: even a steel bar deforms under a large enough force

cards.term: Define elasticity and elastic deformation.
cards.definition: The property by which a body regains its original size and shape when the deforming force is removed

cards.term: Define plasticity. Example?
cards.definition: No tendency to regain shape: the body is permanently deformed. Putty, mud are near-ideal plastics

cards.term: Why does elasticity matter in engineering?
cards.definition: Designing buildings, bridges, cranes, aircraft and artificial limbs needs the elastic properties of steel, concrete etc.

cards.term: Define stress. Unit and dimensions?
cards.definition: Restoring force per unit area, \( \sigma = \dfrac{F}{A} \); N m⁻² = Pa, [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]

cards.term: When a body is deformed, how big is the restoring force?
cards.definition: Equal and opposite to the applied force (body in equilibrium)

cards.term: Stress types and their strains
cards.definition: Tensile / compressive (longitudinal) stress: longitudinal strain ΔL/L; Tangential (shearing) stress: shearing strain Δx/L = tan θ ≈ θ; Hydraulic stress (pressure on all sides): volume strain ΔV/V, no change in shape

cards.term: Identify the four deformations in Fig. 8.1.
cards.definition:
(a) tensile stretching
(b) shear of a cylinder
(c) shear of a book pushed sideways
(d) hydraulic compression of a body in a fluid

cards.term: Why is shearing strain ≈ θ?
cards.definition: For small θ, tan θ ≈ θ (at 10° they differ by only about 1 %)

cards.term: Units of strain?
cards.definition: None: a ratio of like quantities, dimensionless

cards.term: Correction: NCERT says the book-pushing example is "Fig. 8.2(c)". Which figure is it?
cards.definition: Fig. 8.1(c). Fig. 8.2 is the stress–strain curve

cards.term: Is stress a vector (Points to ponder)?
cards.definition: No: it cannot be given a single direction; the force on a given side of a section has a direction

cards.term: A wire hangs from the ceiling with weight F at its end. Tension at a cross-section: F or 2F?
cards.definition: F: the ceiling’s pull balances the weight; stress = F/A

cards.text: Hooke’s law: for small deformations, {{c1::stress ∝ strain}}; the constant of proportionality is the {{c2::modulus of elasticity}}.

cards.term: Is Hooke’s law a fundamental law?
cards.definition: No: it is empirical, valid only in the linear part of the stress–strain curve; some materials never obey it

cards.term: Stress–strain curve of a metal: O, A, B, D, E
cards.definition: O–A linear (Hooke); B yield point/elastic limit; beyond B permanent set; D ultimate strength; E fracture; ductile if D, E far apart

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Stress–strain curve · the story of a stretched wire

A metal wire is loaded more and more until it snaps. Sketch stress vs strain and name the key points.

Label the points as you go.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Stress–strain curve · the story of a stretched wire

A metal wire is loaded more and more until it snaps. Sketch stress vs strain and name the key points.

O–A: linear, Hooke’s law (A = proportional limit). B: yield point / elastic limit (σᵧ).

Beyond B, unloading leaves a permanent set. D: ultimate tensile strength (σᵤ). E: fracture. D and E far apart → ductile; close → brittle.

cards.term: Stress–strain curve, O to A?
cards.definition: Linear: Hooke’s law holds; the body is elastic

cards.term: Stress–strain curve, A to B?
cards.definition: Not proportional, but the body still returns to its original size. B = yield point / elastic limit, stress there = yield strength σᵧ

cards.term: What is a permanent set?
cards.definition: Loaded beyond B and unloaded (e.g. at C), the strain does not return to zero: plastic deformation

cards.term: Ultimate tensile strength and fracture point?
cards.definition: D: maximum stress (σᵤ); beyond it strain grows even with less force, fracture at E

cards.term: Brittle vs ductile from the stress–strain curve?
cards.definition: Brittle: D and E close together (e.g. glass). Ductile: D and E far apart (e.g. copper, mild steel)

cards.term: What are elastomers? Example?
cards.definition: Materials stretched to large strains that still return, without obeying Hooke’s law and with no clear plastic region: rubber, aorta tissue

cards.term: Exercise 8.2: from the given graph, stress 150 × 10⁶ Pa gives strain 0.002. Young’s modulus and yield strength?
cards.definition: Y = 7.5 × 10¹⁰ Pa; yield strength ≈ 3 × 10⁸ Pa

cards.term: Exercise 8.3: A’s curve is steeper and goes higher than B’s. Greater Young’s modulus? Stronger?
cards.definition: A for both: steeper slope → larger Y; higher breaking stress → stronger

cards.term: Define Young’s modulus.
cards.definition: \( Y = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L} \) (tensile or compressive stress ÷ longitudinal strain)

cards.term: Unit of Young’s modulus?
cards.definition: Same as stress: N m⁻² (Pa)

cards.term: Table 8.1: Young’s modulus of steel, copper, aluminium, bone?
cards.definition: Steel 200 GPa, copper 110 GPa, aluminium 70 GPa, bone 9.4 GPa

cards.term: Force to stretch a 0.1 cm² wire by 0.1 %: steel vs aluminium, brass, copper?
cards.definition: Steel 2000 N; Al 690 N, brass 900 N, Cu 1100 N

cards.term: Why is steel called "more elastic" than rubber?
cards.definition: Elasticity is about resisting deformation: steel stretches far less for the same stress (larger Y). "Stretches more = more elastic" is a misconception

cards.term: Exercise 8.4(a): is Young’s modulus of rubber greater than that of steel?
cards.definition: False: steel’s is far greater

cards.term: Exercise 8.4(b): the stretching of a coil spring is determined by which modulus?
cards.definition: Shear modulus (true): the wire of a spring twists rather than stretches

cards.term: Steel rod under tension
cards.definition: Stress 3.18 × 10⁸ Pa, elongation 1.59 mm, strain 0.16 %

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 8.1 · steel rod

Find the missing step.

Steel rod, r = 10 mm, L = 1.0 m, pulled by 100 kN; Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Stress, elongation, strain?
  1. A = π(0.01)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m²
  2. Stress = 10⁵ / 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.18 × 10⁸ Pa
  3. ?
  4. Strain = 1.59 × 10⁻³ = 0.16 %
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 8.1 · steel rod

Find the missing step.

Steel rod, r = 10 mm, L = 1.0 m, pulled by 100 kN; Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Stress, elongation, strain?
  1. A = π(0.01)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m²
  2. Stress = 10⁵ / 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.18 × 10⁸ Pa
  3. ΔL = stress × L / Y = 1.59 × 10⁻³ m
  4. Strain = 1.59 × 10⁻³ = 0.16 %

cards.term: Copper and steel wires in series
cards.definition: Equal stress: ΔLc/ΔLs = 2.5 → ΔLc = 0.5 mm → W ≈ 180 N

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 8.2 · wires in series

Find the missing step.

Copper (2.2 m) and steel (1.6 m) wires, both 3.0 mm diameter, joined end to end; total stretch 0.70 mm. Load?
  1. Same tension and area → Y_c ΔL_c/L_c = Y_s ΔL_s/L_s
  2. ?
  3. ΔL_c = 0.50 mm, ΔL_s = 0.20 mm
  4. W = A Y_c ΔL_c / L_c = 1.8 × 10² N
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 8.2 · wires in series

Find the missing step.

Copper (2.2 m) and steel (1.6 m) wires, both 3.0 mm diameter, joined end to end; total stretch 0.70 mm. Load?
  1. Same tension and area → Y_c ΔL_c/L_c = Y_s ΔL_s/L_s
  2. ΔL_c/ΔL_s = (2.0/1.1)(2.2/1.6) = 2.5
  3. ΔL_c = 0.50 mm, ΔL_s = 0.20 mm
  4. W = A Y_c ΔL_c / L_c = 1.8 × 10² N

cards.term: Example 8.3: circus human pyramid, 220 kg on a performer’s two thighbones (L 0.5 m, r 2.0 cm, Y 9.4 GPa). Compression of each?
cards.definition: 4.55 × 10⁻⁵ m (strain ≈ 0.009 %)

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Examples 8.2–8.4 cite "Table 9.1" and "Eq. (9.8)". What do they mean?
cards.definition: Table 8.1 and Eq. (8.8): references left over from the old chapter numbering

cards.term: Exercise 8.1: steel wire (4.7 m, 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m²) and copper wire (3.5 m, 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ m²) stretch equally under the same load. Y(steel)/Y(copper)?
cards.definition: 1.8 (Y ∝ L/A for equal F and ΔL)

cards.term: Exercise 8.5: steel (1.5 m) holds 4 kg + brass, brass (1.0 m) holds 6 kg; diameter 0.25 cm. Elongations?
cards.definition: Steel 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m (carries 10 kg); brass 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ m

cards.term: Exercise 8.9: steel cable, radius 1.5 cm, stress limit 10⁸ Pa. Maximum load?
cards.definition: F = 10⁸ × π(0.015)² ≈ 7.07 × 10⁴ N

cards.term: Define shear modulus (modulus of rigidity).
cards.definition: \( G = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta x/L} = \dfrac{F}{A\theta} \)

cards.term: Typical relation between G and Y?
cards.definition: \( G \approx \dfrac{Y}{3} \) for most materials

cards.term: Which moduli apply only to solids?
cards.definition: Young’s and shear moduli: only solids have fixed lengths and shapes

cards.term: Example 8.4: lead slab 50 cm × 50 cm × 10 cm, shear force 9.0 × 10⁴ N on the narrow face, lower edge riveted, G = 5.6 GPa. Displacement of the top edge?
cards.definition: Stress = 9.0 × 10⁴ / 0.05 = 1.8 × 10⁶ Pa; Δx = stress × L / G = 0.16 mm

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Example 8.4 writes the stress as 9.4 × 10⁴ N / 0.05 m². What is right?
cards.definition: The force is 9.0 × 10⁴ N (as given); 9.0 × 10⁴ / 0.05 = 1.8 × 10⁶ Pa, which is the value NCERT then uses

cards.term: Exercise 8.6: Al cube, edge 10 cm, one face fixed to a wall, 100 kg hung on the opposite face, G = 25 GPa. Vertical deflection?
Correction: NCERT’s answer key gives 4 × 10⁻⁶ m for Exercise 8.6. Check.
cards.definition: Recomputing: 98 / (2.5 × 10⁸) = 3.92 × 10⁻⁷ m. The key is ten times too large

cards.term: Define bulk modulus.
cards.definition: \( B = -\dfrac{p}{\Delta V/V} \); the minus sign makes B positive, since ΔV < 0 when p rises

cards.term: Define compressibility.
cards.definition: \( k = \dfrac{1}{B} = -\dfrac{1}{\Delta p}\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} \): fractional volume change per unit pressure

cards.term: Order of bulk moduli: solids, liquids, gases?
cards.definition: Solids > liquids ≫ gases; gases are about a million times more compressible than solids

cards.term: Why are solids so incompressible?
cards.definition: Tight coupling between neighbouring atoms; in liquids the coupling is weaker, in gases very weak

cards.term: Which modulus applies to solids, liquids and gases?
cards.definition: Bulk modulus only

cards.term: Bulk modulus of water and of air (STP)?
cards.definition: Water 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa; air 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa

cards.term: Example 8.5: fractional compression of water at the bottom of the Indian Ocean (3000 m)?
cards.definition: p = hρg = 3 × 10⁷ Pa; ΔV/V = p/B = 1.36 %

cards.term: Stress, strain and moduli at a glance (Table 8.4)
cards.definition: Young’s modulus Y (tensile/compressive): shape: yes, volume: no; Shear modulus G: shape: yes, volume: no; Bulk modulus B (hydraulic): shape: no, volume: yes

cards.term: Exercise 8.12: 100.0 L of water compressed by 0.5 L under 100 atm. Bulk modulus? Compare with air.
cards.definition: 2.0 × 10⁹ Pa, about 2 × 10⁴ times that of air (B = p ≈ 10⁵ Pa at constant T): molecules in a liquid are tightly packed

cards.term: Exercise 8.16: pressure change to compress a litre of water by 0.10 %?
cards.definition: Δp = B × 0.001 = 2.2 × 10⁶ Pa

cards.term: Exercise 8.13: density of water at 80.0 atm if 1.03 × 10³ kg/m³ at the surface?
cards.definition: \( \rho = \dfrac{\rho_0}{1 - p/B} \approx \) 1.034 × 10³ kg/m³

cards.term: Define Poisson’s ratio.
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{lateral\ strain}{longitudinal\ strain} = \dfrac{\Delta d/d}{\Delta L/L} \); no units

cards.term: Typical Poisson’s ratio for steel and aluminium alloys?
cards.definition: Steel 0.28–0.30; aluminium alloys ≈ 0.33

cards.term: What is lateral strain?
cards.definition: Strain perpendicular to the applied force (the wire gets thinner as it lengthens)

cards.term: Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire?
cards.definition: \( U = \tfrac12 \dfrac{YAl^2}{L} = \tfrac12 \times \sigma \times \varepsilon \times V \)

cards.term: Elastic energy per unit volume?
cards.definition: \( u = \tfrac12\,\sigma\varepsilon = \tfrac12 Y\varepsilon^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2Y} \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: why is the energy ½ F l, not F l?
cards.definition: The force grows from 0 to F as the wire stretches; the average force is F/2 (triangle under the F–l line)

cards.term: Crane rope for 10 tonnes, mild steel σᵧ = 300 MPa. Minimum area and practical radius?
cards.definition: A ≥ Mg/σᵧ = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ m² (r ≈ 1 cm); with a safety factor of 10, r ≈ 3 cm

cards.term: Why are crane ropes made of many braided thin wires?
cards.definition: For ease of manufacture, flexibility and strength; a single 3 cm wire would be a rigid rod

cards.term: Sag of a beam loaded at the centre?
cards.definition: \( \delta = \dfrac{Wl^3}{4bd^3Y} \)

cards.term: To reduce bending of a beam, increase breadth or depth?
cards.definition: Depth: δ ∝ 1/d³ but only 1/b

cards.term: Why are beams given an I-shaped cross-section?
cards.definition: Enough depth to resist bending, less material and weight, and it avoids buckling of a deep thin bar

cards.term: Pillar with rounded ends vs distributed (flared) ends?
cards.definition: The one with distributed ends supports more load

cards.term: Why can mountains on Earth not be much higher than ~10 km?
cards.definition: At height h the base shear stress ≈ hρg; rock flows beyond ~3 × 10⁸ Pa: h ≈ 3 × 10⁸ / (3 × 10³ × 10) = 10 km

cards.term: Exercise 8.7: four hollow steel columns (radii 30 and 60 cm) share 50 000 kg. Compressional strain of each?
Correction: NCERT’s key gives 2.8 × 10⁻⁶ for Exercise 8.7. Check.
cards.definition: That equals the strain if one column carried the whole load. Shared by four columns, as the question says: 7.2 × 10⁻⁷

cards.term: Chapter 8 concept checks
cards.definition: Hooke’s law holds all the way to the breaking point: False (linear part only); A material that stretches more is more elastic: False; Bulk modulus applies to gases too: True; Stress is a vector: False; A longitudinal stress also changes the width of a wire: True (Poisson’s ratio)

cards.term: Chapter 8 formula sheet
cards.definition: Young’s modulus: Y = FL / (AΔL); Shear modulus: G = F / (Aθ); Bulk modulus: B = −p / (ΔV/V); Elastic energy density: u = ½ stress × strain
